title: Ox, pit, fire (Bava Kamma 2a)
hookLine: the Mishnah opens with four main causes of damage

cards: An ox wanders out of its yard and tramples a neighbor's garden. A man digs a pit in a public path, leaves it open, and someone's donkey falls in.
A farmer lights a fire to burn off his stubble, the wind shifts, and the flames jump into the next field. Three scenes from a farming village, ordinary and a little awful.
They're also the opening of the first gate, tractate Bava Kamma. Before it says anything about money, the Mishnah names the culprits.

teach.b: Ox. Bava Kamma opens: there are four fathers of damage, the ox, the pit, a third that the Talmud argues over, and the fire. You've heard fathers before: last week, the fathers of work on Shabbat.
Same idea here: main categories, with offspring that grow from them.

teach.h: OX, PIT AND FIRE, FROM THE TORAH.
teach.b: First, each one comes from the Torah. The goring ox, and the animal let loose to graze in someone else's field. The pit, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "if a man shall dig a pit and not cover it."
The fire: "he that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution."
Second, the third father is a puzzle. The Mishnah gives it a short, hard word, and in the Talmud one sage says it means a person, another says the tooth, an animal eating what isn't its owner's.
Third, what makes them different? An ox moves on its own. A pit just sits there.
Fire has no life at all, yet it travels. Each causes harm in its own way, so you can't learn one from another. Fourth, what they share, and that's the heart of it.
It's their way to do damage, and guarding them is on you. You didn't trample the garden; your ox did.
You didn't push the donkey; your pit was open. You didn't burn the field; your fire went where fires go. What you set loose in the world, you answer for.
And an ox with a history of goring, the Torah adds, puts even more on its owner, who was warned.

how: Bava Kamma is often among the first tractates studied in yeshivas, and its categories of damage are still applied by rabbinical courts in civil disputes between Jews who bring their cases there.

o: the first father of damage: what you let loose
a sacrifice brought to the Temple for a wrong
a fine paid by whoever starts a field fire

games.q: the fathers of damage — tap the pairs.
p: moves and does harm on its own

s: the Mishnah says the four causes of damage are all alike
it spells out how they differ: an ox moves, a pit sits still, fire has no life yet travels.
the Talmud argues over what the third cause of damage means
one sage says a person, another says the tooth, an animal eating what isn't its owner's.
if you didn't do the harm with your own hands, you owe nothing
the Mishnah says guarding them is on you. what you set loose, you answer for.

games.q: you dug a pit on a path and left it uncovered. your neighbor's donkey fell in. what does the Torah say?
o: the donkey's owner should have watched it.
the one who left the pit open pays.
nobody pays; it was an accident.
games.why: the Torah says the owner of the pit makes it good. the pit was yours, and guarding it was on you.

practice: Walk through your home in your mind: a loose stair rail, a cord across the floor, a candle near a curtain, a dog that slips the gate. Or something less solid, a habit of yours that tends to land on other people.
Find one ox, one pit, one fire that belongs to you, and picture what it would take to guard it.

wordCard.voice: Ox. The first of the four fathers of damage in Bava Kamma: what you own and let loose, you answer for. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: ox, the first of the four fathers of damage in the Mishnah.
